# Marta Kowalczyk — source facts

Status: source reading complete; Marta has not yet confirmed facts or answered questions. No concept or storyboard selected. Source statements below are not cleared for publication.

## Identity and approach

- F01. Name: Marta Kowalczyk. Sources: `material/cv.md`, heading; `material/linkedin.md`, profile.
- F02. Glasgow, Scotland, United Kingdom. Source: `material/linkedin.md`, profile.
- F03. CV title: “Senior Architect, ARB.” LinkedIn title: “Associate at Field & Rowe Architects”; Associate since August 2025. Sources: CV heading; LinkedIn profile and Experience. Public title unresolved.
- F04. Focus: retrofit, timber, housing; works on existing buildings, teaches, and builds small timber things by hand when possible. Source: LinkedIn profile and About. The About paragraph's general carbon claim is a stated position, not a verified statistic for publication.

## Employment and education

- F05. Field & Rowe Architects, 2020–present (CV). LinkedIn: Architect September 2020–August 2025; Associate August 2025–present, Glasgow. Individual responsibilities on projects not provided.
- F06. Architectural Assistant, Brandt Lindgren, Gdansk, 2017–2019. Source: LinkedIn Experience. Individual work, outcomes and public material not supplied.
- F07. Year 2 studio teaching, Clyde School of Architecture, since 2022 (CV); Studio Tutor, September 2022–present, one day per week (LinkedIn Experience). Specific teaching responsibilities not supplied.
- F08. Clyde School of Architecture, part-time MArch, 2019–2021. Source: LinkedIn Education.
- F09. Gdansk Polytechnic Institute, BSc Architecture, 2013–2017. Source: LinkedIn Education.
- F10. Architects Registration Board, registered 2023. Source: LinkedIn Licences. CV also says ARB.

## Projects and figures

- F11. Calder Court, Glasgow: retrofit of 96 flats; completed 2025. Source: CV, Field & Rowe projects. LinkedIn adds 1960s deck-access block, external insulation and new winter gardens. Marta's role and collaborators not specified; project outcome must not be framed as hers alone.
- F12. Calder Court: “68% less heating demand.” Source: LinkedIn Experience. Baseline, measurement/model, time period and attribution unknown.
- F13. Kirk Street, Glasgow: church hall converted to six flats; completed 2023. Sources: CV projects and LinkedIn Experience. Marta's role and collaborators unknown.
- F14. A School That Grows: competition project, shortlisted in 2024; LinkedIn identifies Scottish Timber Schools competition. Sources: CV projects and LinkedIn Experience. Marta's role, team, and whether anything was built unknown; describe as competition only until clarified.
- F15. Cabin at Kashuby, Poland: 28 square metres, timber frame; designed and built with Marta's father, 2021–2022. Source: CV Own Work. Division of work and meaning of area figure unknown. Father's credit/public inclusion preferences unknown.

## Available material (inventory, not actual assets)

- F16. Calder Court: 14 before/after photographs by Tom Reid for Field & Rowe; drawing set including plans, sections and 1:5 wall build-up; before/after heating-demand diagram. Source: `material/images.md`, Calder Court. Photography and employer permissions, drawing authorship and diagram basis unknown.
- F17. Kirk Street: eight photographs by Tom Reid; hall section. Source: images, Kirk Street. Rights, employer permission and section authorship unknown.
- F18. Cabin: approximately 200 of Marta's own photographs from first post to final shingle; every drawing by Marta, hand then CAD; time-lapse of frame erection. Source: images, Cabin. Time-lapse authorship and identifiable people/location restrictions unknown.
- F19. School competition: six submitted A1 boards. Source: images, School competition. Contributors and permission unknown.
- F20. No third-party testimonials, existing website, contact address, or links supplied. Sources: all three material files.

## Gaps

- Intended visitors and desired action at end of page.
- Personal scope, collaborators and credit for firm projects; earlier practice and teaching details if included.
- Definition and provenance of figures, especially heating demand.
- Actual media files; source files suitable for 3D translation are not supplied.
- Rights and privacy boundaries for photography, employer work, competition boards and family participation.
- Daily tools, documents and rituals; influences or formative experiences.
- Contact method and any existing site's future.

## Disagreements

- D01. CV says Senior Architect; LinkedIn says Associate since August 2025. Ask current preferred public title; do not resolve from recency alone.

## To confirm

1. Current public title and whether employment, teaching and registration details are current and correctly stated.
2. Intended audience and desired visitor action/contact method.
3. Marta's individual role on Calder Court, Kirk Street and school competition; team credits; what the competition produced and whether it was built. Earlier practice and teaching scope if these belong on the site.
4. Heating demand reduction: measured or modelled, baseline, time period, scope, author and team attribution. Confirm 96/six flats and completion years.
5. Cabin: confirm area basis, dates and division of work with father; permission to identify/credit him.
6. Permissions/credits for Tom Reid photographs, employer drawings and diagram, hall section and competition boards; creators of drawings, diagram and boards.
7. Cabin time-lapse creator, other people shown, permissions and any location/privacy limits; confirm own photo/drawing inventory.
8. What must not be shown or discussed, including client/occupant details and unpublished work.
9. Everyday working documents, objects and rituals, in Marta's own language.
10. Influences or formative experiences Marta wishes to share.
11. Whether an existing site exists and, if so, its intended future.

## User answers

None yet. All confirmation questions remain open; availability of material does not establish permission.
# Planning handover

Request: plan a distinctive personal portfolio with meaningful 3D and scroll movement, including concept, full scroll, content, colours, typography, mobile and other site requirements. Do not build.

Read: `material/cv.md`, `material/linkedin.md`, `material/images.md`; storyfolio skill and its reading-a-profile reference.

Exists: source fact sheet at `docs/story/facts.md`. Material folder contains text and an asset inventory, not the listed photos/drawings themselves.

Current stop: facts and questions. No answers received; no design selected, storyboard prepared or website built.

Next: record Marta's answers beside the relevant facts; retain unanswered questions. Then read the concept reference, prepare three grounded concepts and a recommendation for Marta's selection. After selection, prepare the complete storyboard with the requested design and practical details. Update handover as decisions arrive.

# The concept

The second stop: from the fact sheet to three concepts the person can choose between.

## What does not work

- A new coat of paint on the same sections.
- 3D as a backdrop behind the text.
- One 3D scene, however good.
- Another site's idea with the names changed.
- A different effect for every section: a wall of jars, then a door that opens, then a scale that tips. Each may be good. Together they are a tour of effects, and nothing carries the visitor from the first to the last.

## Three things to find

**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.

Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.

**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.

"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.

**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.

The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.

## What every form has to hold

Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.

| Role | Holds |
|---|---|
| The opening | Their name, and the question |
| Who | Who is asking |
| Where from | The places and the years |
| How | The way they work |
| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
| What came of it | Outcomes |
| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |

## What the object becomes

In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.

If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.

**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.

## Three concepts, each written like this

Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.

- **The question.**
- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
- **The object,** and its pieces.
- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
- **The opening and the close.**
- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.

Then say which you would choose, and why.

## Test each one before you show it

Rework or drop one that fails.

| Test | Ask |
|---|---|
| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
| Honesty | Does any sentence in it say more than the fact sheet does: a ranking, a reason, which came first, how a thing was left, a day, a place? |
| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |

## Three cases

How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.

**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.

**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.

**An incident review.** Jun is a reliability engineer, also made up. Seven years on call, at a payments company and then at one that books hospital appointments. He wrote his team's incident review template, and gives talks on reviews without blame. His trade's forms: the runbook, the incident review, the on-call handover, the status page, the dashboard. His work is what happens after something breaks, so the form is an incident review: summary, timeline, root cause, action items. A status page is made of tiles, one to a service, so the object is those tiles. The question: "What keeps a system up at 3 a.m.?" Turned down first: a server rack turning, which is the emblem, and a globe of pings behind the text, which is a backdrop.

**An example shows how to reason. Its concept is not taken.** Camille's menu was reasoned from how Camille serves. A chef who sells one loaf a day from a hatch is not a tasting menu. If you find one of these three concepts in your hand for someone else, it has already failed the swap test: it was made for a person who is not in front of you.

In this version a concept is shown in words. There is no engine yet to sketch one on.
# Asking

## Facts

At the first stop your questions go in one message, numbered. `reading-a-profile.md` says what they are.

## A choice

Where you offer a choice, the concept above all, give the ones you would not choose as fully as the one you would. Then say which you would choose, and why.

If the person tells you to choose, choose. Write what you chose, and what you chose it over, into `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`.

## If the person will not answer

Some people will not answer your questions, or will say: decide everything. Then:

- **What is a matter of taste, you decide:** the concept, the look, the order. Say which you chose and what you chose it over.
- **A fact, you do not decide.** What you could not confirm stays off the page. A figure whose meaning you do not know, a project you cannot say ever ran, a paper you cannot say they wrote, a title you cannot say is theirs: leave it out, or carry it in the script marked "to confirm", and stand nothing on it. Build the concept on the facts that needed no confirming. The person's own resume is no exception: if you asked whether a project ever ran and they did not say, "real-time system" is still not confirmed, and it is not printed.
- **Say what is waiting on them,** as a numbered list at the top of what you hand over.

A wrong guess about someone's taste costs them an afternoon. A wrong claim about their work is read by the people they most want to convince, and it is their name on the site, not yours.

# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

item.text: I’ve chosen the drawing set as the strongest direction: location, plans, sections, elevations, details, then schedules. The same six sheets will carry the story as they move from drawings to construction evidence to a clear record of your contributions. Your cabin can provide the visual foundation; Calder Court and the school competition can be explained in text until image permissions are resolved.

item.text:
I’ve chosen **The Drawing Set**: a portfolio that asks, **“How do you turn an architectural idea into something that can be built?”**

One set of six drawing sheets carries the whole page. As you scroll, they reveal relationships between your drawings, construction and finished work, then gather into a complete record. Your own cabin material gives the site its visual identity; your practice contributions are stated precisely.

I considered the RIBA stages and the snag list too. The drawing set gives both prospective clients and schools the clearest introduction, with less explanation and stronger available evidence.

The full [storyboard](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-architect-with-BCaK22/docs/story/storyboard.md) is saved, including individual scroll beats. Nothing has been built.

| Scroll chapter | What visitors see | What moves |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | Your name, Associate role, work focus, cabin proof, and workshop/book influences | An original cabin drawing leads a six-sheet stack that gently assembles |
| **Plans** | Your cabin design and drawings, paired with built photographs | Sheets fan apart so plan and photograph can be compared |
| **Sections** | Structural evidence from the cabin; your structure-and-sections contribution to the school competition, credited to a team of four | Sheets stand as parallel planes, with the relevant face turning toward the reader |
| **Elevations** | Finished cabin photographs and a concise project index with explicit roles | The same sheets arrange into a quiet wall of exhibits |
| **Details** | Drawing-to-construction relationships; your Calder Court responsibility from technical design through handover | Sheets separate into drawing, construction and finished-condition pairs |
| **Schedules** | An orderly record of work, responsibilities and credits, followed by contact | Sheets flatten into a register, then return to the complete set |

Calder Court is always identified as the practice’s project, with the concept attributed to a partner. Your contribution is detailing, wall build-up and site work—not “designed by Marta.”

The chosen look is **warm workshop paper**: off-white `#F3F0E8`, graphite `#242824`, and restrained oxide `#914D35`. Original drawing marks and timber photographs provide texture. **IBM Plex Sans** handles readable headings and prose; **IBM Plex Mono** handles drawing identifiers and technical labels. Shadows and sheet edges give the 3D depth without overwhelming the work.

On a phone, the page becomes a straightforward single-column story with full-width images and short, shallow sheet transitions. There are no long pinned passages or required dragging. Reduced-motion visitors receive static arrangements; without WebGL or JavaScript, all work, attribution, navigation and contact remain accessible.

The first screen supplies your identity, focus, one proof of work and a contact shortcut. Visitors can jump directly to any chapter. The initial site also needs accessible image enlargement, project anchors, credits, search metadata, an owned-image sharing preview, a useful 404 page and a corrected CV before any download is offered.

I assumed English, direct email contact, and one long page initially. Contact would invite **future project conversations** and **guest-critic invitations**, while keeping your current Associate position clear. Standalone case studies, Polish, writing and testimonials can follow when there is material to support them.

Practice photographs, drawings and school boards remain optional additions pending permission. The 68% figure stays out of headline copy until its baseline and scope are specified; any later use must clearly say **modelled**, with no measured in-use result implied. All assumptions are recorded in [decided-for-you.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-architect-with-BCaK22/docs/story/decided-for-you.md).

Please give the storyboard your yes, or tell me what to change. The [storyfolio workflow](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-architect-with-BCaK22/.agents/skills/storyfolio/references/storyboard.md) explicitly ends with “A yes to the script, or what to change.” This is approval of the plan only; your instruction not to build remains in place.
